III. Year 1405. König Władysław von Polen confirms the demarcation of the borders between Poland and the New March. (The Polish heading says: In 1405 König Władysław von Polen confirmed the marking of the borders between Poland and the New March; the German heading says that the King of Poland prescribed the border of the New March.)

Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen and Lithuania, Supreme Prince and heir of Rus’, etc., makes known to all whom it concerns that last year, at the convention held at Pentecost between us and our councillors on the one side, and the venerable and magnificent lord Konrad von Jungingen, Hochmeister of the Order of the Blessed Mary of the German House, and his council on the other, among the other articles and agreements then made, concluded, and written down, these two following articles were to have been inserted in the letters and confirmed by the strength of seals. Through negligence, however, they were omitted from those letters and not inserted among the other articles. Therefore, lest matters so solemnly negotiated and agreed should in any way be deficient or diminished, we have decreed that the same articles be inserted in this present letter. The first is this: concerning the observance of the boundaries, limits, and borders between our lands of Greater Poland and the New March, we promise and pledge to observe those borders and hold them as valid, just as the lord Master and his Order found them at the time they took possession of that land of the New March, and as they had been maintained from ancient times. The second article was this: if it should ever happen that any disputes arise over the boundaries and borders of any lands of the Kingdom of Poland and of the aforesaid Order, those disputes are to be settled and put to rest by friendly agreement. In witness of these matters our seal is attached to this letter. Given at Toruń on Wednesday within the octave of Pentecost, in the year of our Lord 1405, etc.

IV. Year 1406. König Władysław von Polen gives thanks to Konrad von Jungingen, Hochmeister, who sent him falcons as a gift. (The Polish heading says that König Władysław thanks Konrad von Jungingen, Hochmeister for the falcons he sent him as a gift.)

Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen and Lithuania, Supreme Prince and heir of Rus’, etc., to the magnificent and venerable lord Konrad von Jungingen, Hochmeister of the Order of the Hospital of the Blessed Mary of the German House in Prussia, our sincerely beloved friend: greetings and the fullness of charity in the love of Christ. Magnificent and venerable lord, our sincerely beloved friend: the welcome dispatch of your falcons, now brought to us, has brought us such great joy and comfort that it cannot be expressed in writing. In this gift we consider not only the greatness of the present, but the affection of the friend who sent it, dearer than all gifts or offerings. For this we rise to offer you thanks to be impressed upon your memory repeatedly and for ever. Would that our mind were wise and could foresee what would make your mind glad or acquire for you suitable gifts of consolation; this would indeed bring us special comfort. Although we are quite confident of the wholly sincere affection you bear us, we would be still more confident and much more secure if, without presuming on our account, you would take care to ask us to acquire for you whatever would please you and could be found in the lands under our rule. Accordingly, we earnestly ask your sincerity that, setting aside all hesitation, you boldly request from us whatever would be acceptable to you and could be found under our authority, so that we may freely send it to you. Given at Poznań on Friday, the day after Corpus Christi, in the year of our Lord 1406. By the report of Nicholas, provost of Saint Florian before Kraków, vice-chancellor of the Kingdom of Poland.

To the magnificent and venerable lord Konrad von Jungingen, Hochmeister of the Order of the Hospital of the Blessed Mary of the German House, bearer of the Cross in Prussia, our sincerely beloved friend.

V. Year 1407. Władysław, König von Polen, congratulates Ulrich von Jungingen, Hochmeister when he attained the dignity of Grand Master of the Teutonic Order. (The Polish heading says that König Władysław congratulates Ulrich von Jungingen, Hochmeister on his elevation to the dignity of Grand Master.)

To the venerable lord von Jungingen, Master General of the Order of the German House in Prussia, our beloved friend. Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen, etc.

Venerable lord, our sincerely beloved friend: from the reports and information of our friends we have learned that your friendship has, by divine favor, been raised to the seat of the supreme mastership of the German House of the Order of the Blessed Virgin Mary in Prussia. We rejoice at this from the depths of our heart all the more gladly, inasmuch as we fully trust in the Lord that your friendship will steadfastly follow the footsteps of your brother and predecessor, the lord Konrad von Jungingen of blessed memory, who was bound to our Majesty and Kingdom by the firm bond of charity and peace. But because, in the affairs of the Crown and our Kingdom, we are sending to your friendship the most reverend father in Christ, lord Nicholas, Erzbischof zu Gniezno, and our faithful and beloved valiant lord Jan of Chełmce, castellan of Kalisz, who are fully informed of our intentions, with this letter we ask that your friendship give credence to what they say on our behalf, as if we ourselves were speaking in person with your friendship. We also ask that you summon your senior councillors to hear our intentions, informing them through the bearer of this letter on which day and at what place they may meet your friendship. Given at Łęczyca on the eve of the Visitation of the glorious Virgin Mary.

VI. Year 1409. The King of Poland gives thanks to Ulrich von Jungingen, Hochmeister, who sent him eight falcons as a gift. (The Polish heading likewise says that the King thanks Ulrich von Jungingen for sending him eight falcons as a gift.)

Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen and Lithuania, Supreme Prince and heir of Rus’, etc., to the magnificent and venerable lord Ulrich von Jungingen, Hochmeister of the Order of the Hospital of the Blessed Mary of the German House, bearer of the Cross in Prussia, our sincerely beloved friend: greetings and the increase of sincere favor. Magnificent and venerable lord, our sincerely beloved friend: for the gifts already given and greatly accepted, namely eight falcons and a gyrfalcon sent to us by your sincerity at a suitable time, we rise to give you thanks, to be recalled repeatedly and for a long time. Yet we value not so much their preciousness as the affection of heartfelt charity that you bear us in pure faith, which we consider dearer than all gifts. Therefore we earnestly ask your sincerity that you be willing to ask us boldly, without any scruple of shame, for the things pleasing to us which the extent of our Kingdom and the lands of Lithuania and Rus’ contain and in which they may be found, so that, upon obtaining them, we may gladly send them to you. By this you will show us a more perfect friendship. Given at Sandomierz on Wednesday after the Sunday Invocavit, in the year of our Lord 1409. By the report of Nicholas, provost of Saint Florian, vice-chancellor of the Kingdom of Poland.

To the magnificent and venerable lord Ulrich von Jungingen, Hochmeister of the Order of the Hospital of the Blessed Mary of the German House, bearer of the Cross in Prussia, our sincerely beloved friend, etc.

VII. Year 1409. The King of Poland informs the commander of Toruń of the arrival of his envoys. (The Polish heading says: The King of Poland reports to the commander of Toruń the arrival of his envoys.)

To the venerable lord Schwarzenburg, Commander of Toruń, our beloved friend. Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen, etc. Venerable friend, our beloved: in answer to the matters of your embassies, concerning which you wrote to us on behalf of the Grand Master and your Order, we have decided to send to that same Grand Master the reverend father in Christ, lord Nicholas, by God’s grace Archbishop of Gniezno, together with the noble and valiant lords Matthias, Palatin zu Kalisz, and Wincenty of Granów, Kastellan zu Nakło, our faithful and beloved knights. Accordingly, we ask and exhort your sincerity to deliver to the Master the letter addressed to him which we send to you with this present letter, and to write him a special letter of your own concerning the matter, informing our aforesaid envoys where and when they should meet with him. Given at Łęczyca on Friday, the day after Saint Arnold’s day, in the year of our Lord 1409. By the report of Nicholas, Vice-Chancellor of the Kingdom of Poland.

VIII. Year 1409. The Grand Master of the Teutonic Order instructs his commander to complain to the King of Poland that Vytautas, Herzog has sent his governor into Samogitia contrary to the agreements. (The Polish heading says that the Grand Master orders the commander to complain to the Polish King about Vytautas, Herzog von Litauen, who sent his governor to Samogitia contrary to the treaties.)

The Grand Master. Dear lord Commander, as we wrote to you recently concerning the business you are to conduct with the King of Poland, and in particular wrote that we had heard that Vytautas, Herzog had appointed a captain for the Samogitians, from which we infer that the treachery was committed with his consent and at his instigation, etc., we have since given much thought to this, and it seems better to us that you present the matter in a qualified and careful way: say that we have heard Vytautas, Herzog appointed a captain for the Samogitians, and ask who that person is. In that way the Master can infer nothing other than that the treachery was committed with his consent. Thus, do not accuse Vytautas, Herzog of the treachery outright, but qualify your words as to whether he appointed a captain among them. And, dear lord Commander, be careful in all your words to speak in this same way, so that Vytautas, Herzog may not later accuse us of such a thing, if perhaps the matter is otherwise or he should speak differently, since we do not yet know the whole truth about it. Given at Marienburg on the feast of Saints Vitus and Modestus, in the year nine [1409].

To the Commander at Toruń. It travelled day and night without delay from Marienburg on Saint Vitus’ day, leaving at twelve o’clock at noon. It arrived there on the Sunday after Saint Vitus, when the clock had struck twelve, and at that same hour continued onward toward midnight. It arrived at Engelsberg between three and four, then departed again from there between three and four. It reached the Lippe on the Sunday after Saint Vitus, when the clock had struck eight in the morning, and at that same hour continued onward.

IX. Year 1409. Complaints of the Poles against the Teutonic Order concerning the castles and towns of Drezdenko, Santok, and others. (The Polish heading likewise refers to Polish complaints against the Order concerning the castles and towns of Drezdenko and Santok.)

The following articles were presented by the envoys of the Lord King of Poland to the Grand Master and his council, and urged upon them. Thereafter follow the Grand Master’s answers and those of his council. This took place at Elbląg on the Monday after Corpus Christi, in the year 1409.

First, concerning the castle of Drezdenko, which the Order had taken in pledge during the aforesaid perpetual peace, and after taking it had bought for itself, although that castle, with its lordship, had belonged to the Crown of Poland for all time; they had never dared to reclaim it, and had continually excused themselves to the König von Ungarn. Our answer is that Drezdenko, with its appurtenances and jurisdiction, belonged to the New March, according to the direction of the Lord König von Ungarn and the hereditary charters granted of old by the Margraves over Drezdenko. The Order took that castle in pledge from Lord Ulrich under such conditions that, when it was returned to him, he was to provide reasonable security that he would not alienate the castle from the New March. Meanwhile, the Lord König von Ungarn addressed the Grand Master and the Order, admonishing them earnestly to keep Drezdenko within the New March, saying that he would hold them to account for it. Since Lord Ulrich could not provide the Order with adequate security concerning Drezdenko, and would no longer allow it to remain in pledge, the Order had to buy it from him. If the Order is to keep it within the New March under the command of the Lord König von Ungarn, the Order has not agreed to keep it for ever; rather, whoever is adjudged to have the right, to that person the Order is willing to surrender or hand it over for as much money as it paid for it, so that the Order may preserve its honor.

The second article concerns Santok Castle, which the Grand Master had promised to the Lord King of Poland and Vytautas, Herzog on the day at Kovno, saying that he would not take possession of it. Now he has taken possession of the castle and forgotten his promise. Our answer: we acknowledge that we said we would not take possession of Santok, although we had always heard that Santok belonged to the New March from ancient times. As soon as we came home, we wrote to the Vogt of the New March that we had heard certain reports. He had the bailiff, men, and townspeople informed; they met together about it and answered the Vogt that Santok had belonged to the New March from of old. That Santok belongs to the New March is shown by what happened when we returned from the day at Kovno with the King of Poland and Vytautas, Herzog: we were detained, and on the advice of our lords we sent our messenger, the Commander of Balga, to the König von Ungarn. As our messenger was about to set out, we informed Sir Johanniter, the lord who held Santok in possession and in pledge on behalf of his Order, and who went with the Commander of Balga to the King. When they both came to the King—the Commander of Balga and the Johanniter lord—the Commander of Balga spoke to our lord the König von Ungarn on our behalf, saying that the King of Poland had Santok Castle and Drezdenko Castle in pledge. The King replied, “My gracious lord King, from you and no one else.” Then he said to the Johanniter: “Do you acknowledge that the Johanniter said this?” “Yes, great and mighty lord.” We commanded and earnestly instructed him to place Santok Castle under the protection of the Master of Prussia, just as the New March had been given into our protection by you; and if Santok Castle were alienated from the New March, or any damage or hindrance were done to it, we would seek compensation from you and your whole Order for our loss.

The third article concerns Jan, Herzog von Masowien: the Order burned the Duke’s villages within his borders, and the Order built its own houses in that Duke’s land, burning villages without waiting for the judgments agreed at Kovno, where Vytautas, Herzog had ridden there with the Commander of Elbląg and the Commander of Balga. Our answer: the burned villages were within our borders, which we have held for a long time. The Duke of Masovia was warned by our council that he should not rebuild or allow people to dwell there; this was not permitted to him. He then sought to gain a foothold within our borders by force; since he would not desist, his villages were burned so that he should have no claim to them. This too was said at Kovno. We still offer, as we have often done, that whenever our lord Vytautas, Herzog wishes to ride there with our lords, we will accept whatever is established there according to the evidence and to Duke Jan’s reasonable acknowledgment. If he willingly agrees to this, we would not wish to hinder him in anything to which he has a right, once that right has been shown to us in like manner.

The fourth article: merchants from the Kingdom of Poland were forbidden to carry their merchandise toward the sea, contrary to the old custom. Our answer: we would gladly maintain the old custom if our lord the King would likewise allow our people, according to old custom, to travel through the Kingdom of Poland with their merchandise. Just as this was allowed in the time of his forefathers, so we are willing to allow the people of his Kingdom to travel likewise toward the sea and everywhere through our land.

The fifth article: the people of Brandenburg were forbidden to carry rye, pitch, ashes, and certain other goods to Danzig in large ships, being permitted to do so only in small ships and no farther than Świecie, where they are also forbidden to sell them. Our answer: when the people of Brandenburg were with us and complained about this, we wrote to the Commander at Świecie that he should allow them to travel and sell their goods, using the same kinds of ships as they had used of old. If anything has been wrongfully withheld from them in this matter, let both our words be brought forward; if it is acknowledged that the fault lies with us or our people, we will make amends, and in all matters will deal with them as has been done of old.

The sixth article: the Order had built a mill at Lubiesz on the King’s bank, and then held both banks firmly at the bridgehead, and also took some meadows and islands and dug them in on the King’s side. Our answer: when both our statements about this are heard, if the Order has acted against any reasonable possession for which it has neither evidence nor right, we are willing to give it up; likewise, we trust that our lord the King will not hinder the Order in its ancient and reasonable possession.

The seventh article: the people of Toruń wished to have a free fishing ground in the lower Vistula, from which they had previously provided fish to the King of Poland. Our answer: when the matter is examined, if it is acknowledged that the people of Toruń have a right to it, they shall be given it according to the old custom.

The eighth article: the Commander of Bierzgłowo had, at Toruń, a fish-trap in the Vistula for a permanent fishery, which the King had granted him for one year. Our answer: if it is acknowledged that he is wrongfully claiming something that was never granted to him of old, he shall relinquish it. Likewise, we trust that our lord the King will allow our Order what it has a right to, according to old custom.

The ninth article: the people of Fordon on the river had twice been wounded and struck down. Our answer: we know nothing of this, but if our people have done them any wrong, they shall make amends according to what both sides acknowledge.

The tenth article: the Vogt of the New March had made a new boundary within the Kingdom of Poland, three miles wide and ten miles long, beyond the old border of Drezdenko Castle; he says it belongs to Drezdenko Castle and claims that the Grand Master ordered him to do it. Our answer: we know nothing of this, nor did we order the Vogt to do it. But if it pleases our lord the King, let him send two or three surveyors—or as many as he thinks good—to inspect the boundary. We are willing to do the same, so that both sides may acknowledge the matter according to the testimony of the old inhabitants and the evidence and charters. If the Order has taken possession of anything that belongs to the Kingdom of Poland, we are willing to relinquish it. Whatever they acknowledge has belonged of old to Drezdenko and the New March, we trust that our lord the King will not hinder our Order from holding.

The eleventh article: the Commander of Tuchel had imprisoned Jakob von Rieverse in the church at Kamenetz on account of a debt owed to one of the King’s men. Our answer: we do not know the matter so precisely; but when our word reaches there and we investigate it, if it is acknowledged that the Commander has done wrong, he shall make amends.

X. Year 1409. The Order’s High Marshal informs the Grand Master that Vytautas is anxious lest the Order attack him. (The Polish heading says the highest marshal of the Order reports to the Grand Master that Vytautas fears the Order may attack him.)

My willing and humble service beforehand. Venerable, dear lord Master, may Your Venerability know that, while this letter was being written, the Vogt’s messenger from Samogitia came to the Commander of Balga. He says that Vytautas, Herzog is greatly afraid that you may march into his land with a small force, so that he would have neither Rusyns nor Tatars with him. He also says that he has Swidrigaila with him, but by God’s grace and counsel does not invite him to his table or his council. Vytautas, Herzog has gone to the King of Poland with few men. We can learn no other news of him. Given at Ełk on the Sunday after the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, in the year 1409. The High Marshal.

To the Venerable Grand Master, without delay, day or night, with all due respect, etc.

XI. Year 1409. The King of Poland declares that, in order to preserve peace with Swidrigaila, he will appoint and hold a meeting with him. The heading gives the date as Troki, three days before Saint Martin’s feast, in the year 1430 (Capsa XXIII, no. 17).

Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen and Lithuania, Supreme Prince and heir of Rus’, etc., makes known by this letter to all whom it concerns that, desiring to remain more securely in brotherly affection and perfect charity with the illustrious prince, lord Bolesław, also called Swidrigaila, Grand Duke of Lithuania, etc., our dearest brother, and to govern more fully in peace and tranquility the lands of our Kingdom of Poland, we have undertaken, and by this letter undertake and establish, a day of meeting with that same Grand Duke at the coming feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, at the place or places which we, with our men, and the Grand Duke, with his barons, shall determine. At that place and appointed time, we and the Grand Duke wish and are bound to attend and meet, together with the full council of the elders and senior men of each of us; there we shall seek and carefully investigate on both sides all matters necessary and useful for the peace, friendship, unity, and concord of us both and of the aforesaid lands of our Kingdoms of Poland and Lithuania. Meanwhile, we, Władysław, König von Polen, etc., promise in good faith, on our royal word, without deceit or fraud, on behalf of ourselves and our people, to live and remain in peace and tranquility, permitting or beginning no wars, devastations, or plundering in either of our lands. Rather, in perfect charity, friendship, peace, and tranquility, we faithfully promise to remain until the meeting. In witness of this letter our seal is attached. Done and given at Troki on Tuesday before the feast of Saint Martin, in the year of our Lord 1430, etc.

In the seventh week before the appointed day of meeting with the King, the Poles broke the peace with the Lithuanians.

XII. Year 1409. Władysław, König von Polen, promises to accept the arbitral decision of Wenceslaus, King of Bohemia, in the disputes that arose between Poland and the Teutonic Order. The aforesaid King of Poland also promises to uphold the peace concluded by his predecessor, King Casimir. (The Polish headings repeat these points.)

We, Władysław, by God’s grace King of Poland, Supreme Prince of Lithuania and heir of Rus’, etc., acknowledge and make known to all who see, hear, or read this letter that the most illustrious prince and lord, lord Wenceslaus, by God’s grace König der Römer for all time and King of Bohemia, our dear brother, has sent the high-born princes and lords, lord Konrad the Elder and lord Konrad, his son, called Senior, by the grace of God dukes in Silesia and lords of Olesno and Koźle; and the noble brothers Wenceslaus and Niemysł of Donyn; Jan of Chotěmice, captain of Wrocław and Świdnica; Hans von Schwein, knight; and the honorable and wise councilmen of the city of Wrocław, his princes, councillors, and beloved faithful men, to undertake such wars, hostilities, disputes, and disagreements as we have had, and still have, with the venerable spiritual lord Ulrich von Jungingen, Hochmeister of the Teutonic Order, and his whole Order. With great, faithful, and diligent effort and care, they have negotiated, arranged, and made between us on one side and the aforesaid Grand Master and his Order on the other a firm, strong, and inviolable Christian peace, on behalf and in the name of the aforesaid most illustrious prince and lord Wenceslaus, König der Römer and Bohemia, our dear brother, in the manner written below.

First, we promise to have and keep with the aforesaid lord Grand Master and his Order a firm, strong, and inviolable Christian peace until the next feast of Saint John the Baptist, in all respects and according to all the points and articles contained here, just as the former peace was agreed, made, and confirmed with King Casimir of blessed memory, without evasion. We have also submitted all our disputes, disagreements, grievances, and hostilities with the aforesaid lord Grand Master and his Order—our complaints and accusations and their answers, as well as their complaints and our answers—to the aforesaid lord Wenceslaus, König der Römer and Bohemia, our dear brother, for his authoritative decision. Whatever he, with his wise council and those whom he may further choose, pronounces between us, we shall faithfully hold and observe firmly and without breach for all time; and we pledge by this letter and our royal word to observe his decision firmly and without breach in every matter, point, and article, without deceit or evasion. The aforesaid lord Wenceslaus, König der Römer and Bohemia, our dear brother, is to make his decision between the two parties by the next Fastnacht, on the day and at the place he shall notify to both parties. If we cannot come there in person, we may send our representatives in our name and place, with full authority to follow and accept such decision as if we ourselves were present, without evasion.

All fortresses and lands, with every appurtenance, which either party possesses on this day, shall be freely and without hindrance held, possessed, and enjoyed by each side until the decision of the aforesaid brother, without evasion. Any knights, squires, country folk, townspeople, or peasants who have fled their homesteads and property during this war and wish to return to them, we promise to let return freely and remain there until the decision, provided that meanwhile they do to us what is proper and right, without evasion. We also grant all prisoners a safe-conduct and promise not to summon them to fight before the decision.

We further promise, without excluding or excepting anyone, to keep the aforesaid peace unbroken with all kings, princes, counts, nobles, lords, knights and squires, burghers and peasants, clergy and lay people who have come or may come to the aid of the Grand Master and the Order in this war and conflict, and with all who have given them counsel and assistance. We shall observe that peace in every respect, just as we are to keep it with the Grand Master and his Order, without deceit or evasion. We also pledge on our royal word that we shall give the Samogitians and all other non-Christians, and all their helpers, no counsel, aid, or support, and shall not in any way take their part, nor shall we receive them into our peace in any manner, without deceit or evasion.

We pledge on our royal word to keep firmly and without alteration all the aforesaid peace terms, agreements, and promises in every respect in which they have been set out and written, without deceit or evasion. For greater assurance, we, the aforesaid councillors, namely Nicholas, by God’s grace Archbishop of Gniezno; Nicholas, lord of Wojnicz; Jan, lord of Kalisz; Zbigniew, Marschall of the Kingdom of Poland; Piotr Szafraniec, under-treasurer of Kraków; Dobrogost Świdwa; Matthias, voivode of Kalisz; Wincenty of Granów, lord of Nakło; and Nicholas of Opole, have pledged before the aforesaid most illustrious prince and lord Władysław, König von Polen, our beloved lord, in his presence and together with him, to keep all the aforesaid peace terms, agreements, and arrangements in every clause, point, and article firmly, wholly, without breach or alteration, and without deceit or evasion. God forbid that the aforesaid peace, terms, or agreements should in any way be broken by us or our people. If they are broken, the aforesaid most illustrious prince and lord Wenceslaus, König der Römer and Bohemia, our dear brother, shall and may assist and support the Grand Master and the Order against us, our Kingdom, as he sees fit, as we and our people have violated the peace; he may fully remedy the breaches committed by us or our people according to his own judgment. Neither the King nor anyone whom he has commissioned or may commission to do such a thing on his behalf shall be hindered or harmed for it in any way, without deceit or evasion.

In witness and confirmation of this, we have attached our royal seal to this letter, and each of the aforesaid councillors has attached his own seal. Given on the border between Świecie and Bydgoszcz, on the Tuesday after the feast of Saint Francis, in the year of our Lord 1409. (The parchment is covered with many stains.)

XIII. Year 1409. Alliance of Sigismund, König von Ungarn, with Ulrich von Jungingen, Hochmeister, against the King of Poland. (The Polish heading says that Sigismund, König von Ungarn, formed an alliance with Ulrich Jungingen, Hochmeister, against the King of Poland.)

We, Sigismund, by the grace of God König von Ungarn, Dalmatia, Croatia, Rama, Serbia, Galicia, Lodomeria, Cumania, and Bulgaria, Margrave of Brandenburg, Vicar-General and Chamberlain of the Holy Roman Empire, and heir of Bohemia and Luxembourg, acknowledge by this present letter before all that, for the honor and glory of almighty God, and for the growth and strength of the whole orthodox faith, and for the peace, tranquility, welfare, and advancement of our kingdoms and subjects of every status and condition; and especially because we have always had, and still have, sincere devotion to the worthy and religious Order of Brothers of the German House; and further observing that they and their lands serve as a defense and shield for Christ’s faithful on their borders, while we and our kingdoms do so on the other side against the infidels; after deliberate and mature consideration and sufficient counsel, and with certain knowledge, we have resolved to make a true union and particular leagues and confederations with the venerable lord brother Ulrich von Jungingen, Hochmeister of the aforesaid Order of the German House, his successors, and the whole Order. The worthy and religious brothers Werner von Tettingen, Grand Hospitaller and Commander at Elbląg, and Albert, Graf von Schwarzburg, Commander at Toruń, were sent to our Majesty by the Hochmeister in the name of himself and his whole Order as their true and lawful procurators and envoys, with full commission and complete authority; and by the force of this letter we make the agreements set out below.

First and principally: if at any time hereafter any quarrels or wars should arise, for whatever reason, between Władysław, König von Polen, or his heirs and successors, the Kings of Poland, and the aforesaid Kingdom of Poland on one side, and the aforesaid Hochmeister, his successors, and his Order on the other; and if that King of Poland, his heirs and successors, the Kingdom of Poland, or their allies should receive or take as their aid and support against the aforesaid Hochmeister, his successors, and his Order infidels such as Lithuanians, Ruthenians, Tatars, or any other schismatics and persons separated from the Holy Roman Church, by whatever names they may be called, and should wish to harm, molest, or in any way impede the Hochmeister and Order with those infidels; and if we, our heirs, or successors, Kings of Hungary, or our aforesaid Kingdom of Hungary are called upon by the aforesaid Hochmeister, his successors, or the Order under this agreement, then immediately, without any delay, we wish, promise, and are bound to assist the same Hochmeister and Order with all our strength against the aforesaid King of Poland, his heirs and successors, Kings of Poland, the aforesaid Kingdom of Poland, and their allies, without deceit or fraud. We shall faithfully provide them such aid or support along the borders and marches of our aforesaid Kingdom of Hungary, or wherever we can do so better and more advantageously, in every event, whether gain or loss, without deceit or fraud. If, in such quarrels or wars arising as aforesaid, we happen to recover lands and possessions alienated from the Order, or occupied and usurped by the aforesaid King of Poland or the Kingdom of Poland, we shall then restore and yield those lands and possessions that we have recovered to the aforesaid Order, and shall in no way retain them against that Order.

Furthermore, whenever in the future quarrels or wars arise between the aforesaid Hochmeister, his successors, and the Order on one side, and the aforesaid King of Poland, his heirs and successors, Kings of Poland, or the Kingdom of Poland on the other, while those quarrels and wars continue we shall neither make nor maintain any truce or peace agreement with the aforesaid King of Poland, his heirs and successors, or the Kingdom of Poland without the knowledge and consent of the aforesaid Hochmeister, his successors, and the Order. Rather, we wish and are bound faithfully to assist the Hochmeister and Order against the aforesaid King of Poland, his heirs and successors, and the Kingdom of Poland, in the manner set out above.

If, however, we, the aforesaid König Sigismund of Hungary, or our heirs or successors, Kings of Hungary, or the aforesaid Kingdom of Hungary should happen to enter into any disputes with the aforesaid King of Poland, his heirs or successors, or the Kingdom of Poland over borders, boundaries, lands, people, or any other cause, and should be able to obtain due satisfaction and agreement from them in that matter, whenever this occurs in the future we shall be permitted to accept such satisfaction, but only wholly without prejudice to the union, leagues, and confederations set out above. Such an agreement shall in no way violate or infringe them; rather, all their clauses and articles stated above shall be observed perpetually and inviolably. In any such agreement or settlement that we may make in the manner aforesaid, we must expressly except and declare that we wish to observe forever, wholly unharmed and inviolate, the union and all the leagues and confederations made and established with the aforesaid Hochmeister and Order. We, the aforesaid Sigismund, König von Ungarn, promise in good faith, on our royal word and without deceit or fraud, on behalf of ourselves, our heirs and successors, Kings of Hungary, and our aforesaid Kingdom of Hungary, to keep the aforesaid union, leagues, and confederations firm and intact in all their clauses and articles and to observe them inviolably for all time. In witness of this letter our seal of Majesty is attached. Given at Buda in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1409, on Friday, the eve of Saint Thomas the Apostle.

Diplomatic acts during the reign of Władysław Jagiełło, for the year 1410.

I. Year 1410. An unknown person informs the Grand Master what has been reported to him about the court of the Queen of Poland. (The Polish heading says an unnamed person informs the Hochmeister what he has heard about the Polish Queen’s court.)

To the venerable, most mighty lord, lord Hochmeister of the Teutonic Order, his princely grace: may this letter be received with great respect, etc. My willing and humble service, always without fail. Venerable, dear, gracious lord, I inform Your Princely Grace that I was at the court of the gracious Queen, may God have her in his keeping, with young Cretkoffken, whose father was a captain and voivode over all Kuyavia, from the last Saint Martin’s day onward. Then news came to the Queen that the Tatars had again done great damage near Lutsk, and the messenger said the Tatars had no hindrance from the Poles. I have also heard at the Queen’s court that the Poles were in Silesia before Fastnacht, plundered there, and then rode out again. I have also heard at the Queen’s court that the Poles greatly praise the Silesians, saying they are fierce, combative people and bite back hard. Your Princely Grace should also know that the Polish captains who sit on the border toward Silesia—such as Szarwiński, lord Saramba, and lord Drzyrski—have bands of robbers with them and must rob; the Polish captains pass through the border districts, and the Silesians will not tolerate it, so they ride out toward Kraków and retaliate wherever they can. Your Princely Grace should also know that the Poles are greatly troubled, because they cannot conclude any meeting without the Bishop of Kraków, who could not attend any meeting, and the Archbishop is gravely ill; it is feared that he will die of it. Now the Poles wish to hold a meeting with the King at Brześć on Saint George’s day, while the King wishes to hold it on Saint John the Baptist’s day; thus they remain continually at odds. When I learn a firmly appointed day, I shall let Your Princely Grace know without delay. I have no one on earth to whom I can complain of my great suffering and poverty except Your Princely Grace. This drives me to place my hope in God and in Your Princely Grace’s help, that you may help a poor man with bread in my old age and sustain my life. Your Princely Grace should also know that the Poles wish to wage war wherever they can; this is not yet publicly known at this time. I pray God for Your Princely Grace’s health and for the whole Order. Good night. N. S.

II. Year 1410. An unknown person informs the Grand Master of disputes that arose between the King of Poland and the nobles of his kingdom. (The Polish heading says an unnamed person informs the Hochmeister of conflicts between the Polish King and his lords.)

To the venerable, mighty lord, lord Hochmeister of the Teutonic Order, his princely grace: may this letter be received with great respect. My willing and humble service at all times, without fail. Venerable, dear, gracious lord, I inform Your Princely Grace of news from the discussion at Piotrków: the King has agreed with the Poles that they should raise a defensive force at Kamieniec in Podolia against the Tatars. In return, the King’s own court household is to be exempted for one year. Your Princely Grace should also know that the King has made a four-year peace with the princes of Silesia, because the Lithuanians do not wish to surrender the land of Lutsk; the Poles wish by this means to have a better chance of obtaining their will from the Lithuanians, for the Poles intend to have Lutsk or to die for it. The Poles have also pressed the King strongly concerning the royal word he gave them, that he would let them retain their ancient rights. The King is now holding them to it. The Poles rebuked him so severely that he cried out in answer: “I know well that you do not want me for your King, and are thinking how you might depose me.” Thus they parted from the King without agreement, and the Poles went into council. Then the Lithuanians sent a Lithuanian who looked just like a Pole. When the Poles recognized him, they struck the King as an insult and shouted that his life had only just been spared. The Queen then intervened in the matter with great vehemence, so that the King did the Poles’ will, though it could not be done at that time. Then the Lithuanians departed from Poland. Your Grace should also know that the King is to take the Emperor’s sister as his wife. All the lords, spiritual and secular, are to come to Kraków on Saint Alexius’s day and choose the spiritual and secular men who are to go to the Emperor for the Emperor’s sister. The departure is to take place on Saint James’s day, and the King is to stay at Kraków until they bring the young woman to him. A tax has been imposed by the King on the burghers: one groschen on each mark and six groschen on every hide of land; this money is to be the Queen’s morning gift. There is also disagreement over who is to be Archbishop, for it is not yet known for certain who it will be. Gracious lord, I would gladly speak more fully with Your Grace about these matters, but Your Princely Grace knows more than I can write. I can write no more at this time. I pray God to grant Your Grace great health. Good night. N. S.

On the enclosed note: I also ask Your Princely Grace to accept as excused that I do not write Your Grace at length as my gracious lord; God knows that I have no one near me but Nicolaus Beyrse, who lives not far from me, and he has been greatly wronged and driven out of Prussia. Therefore I ask Your Princely Grace, my beloved gracious lord, to support me at this time with a contribution through my dear lord Kunter of Toruń.

III. Year 1410. Jakub, Bischof von Płock, asks Ulrich von Jungingen, Hochmeister, not to damage the church’s properties situated in the land of Dobrzyń.

To the magnificent and venerable lord brother Ulrich von Jungingen, Hochmeister of the Order of the Hospital of the Teutonic Brothers of the Blessed Mary. Magnificent and venerable lord, lover of justice: last year, when the storm of war was raging because of the sins of men, I humbly entreated Your Magnificence not to devastate the property of my church. I and all clergy are outside that storm, unable to take part in it; we ought to harm no one and benefit everyone. You kindly granted my request, and by your just, gracious, and prudent provision protected my property in the land of Dobrzyń and elsewhere, allowing it to remain safe. You had also generously written to the Commander at Ostróda that he likewise should not lay waste to the aforesaid property. Therefore, if he whose task it is to establish peace in the lands and show mercy to the poor does not look down from above upon this storm of war and does not stop it, but allows this storm to extend into bitter rains, I humbly beseech you again: considering the foregoing, do not permit your armies to ravage my church’s property, but protect it as a matter of justice. Write and command the Commanders at Ostróda, Strasburg, and elsewhere likewise not to devastate my church’s property but to protect it, and graciously send me a reply concerning these matters. May you receive long life in this world from the Most High, and eternal life among the blessed in the world to come. Płock, the seventh day of June. Jakub, by the grace of God Bischof von Płock.

IV. Year 1410. Letter of the King of Poland to the people of Toruń and other towns situated in the land of Chełmno, urging them to submit voluntarily.

Copy of the letter of the King of Poland, delivered to the citizens of the city of Toruń on the Sunday before the feast of Mary Magdalene, in the year 1410. Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen, Prince of Lithuania and heir of Rus’, etc., to the prudent men, masters of the citizens, councillors, and rectors of Toruń and the other cities of the land of Chełmno, sincere and beloved by us: grace and an increasing continuance of favor. Prudent men, sincerely beloved by us, know that on Tuesday, the holy feast of the Division of the Apostles, we fought a battle and engagement against the Hochmeister and his Order, who had not hesitated to break the perpetual peace treaties with us and our Kingdom and had inflicted other injuries upon us; by the power of the Most High we defeated and overthrew them. There the Hochmeister, your own, and the Marshal, with many of his fellow commanders, perished by the sword. Therefore, lest we cause you and your property still greater harm through fires and losses—which, against our will and with all distress, we would be compelled to do—we earnestly request your whole community to give and render us the homage of allegiance, so that such losses may be brought to an end. We, for our part, wish firmly to preserve all your rights, immunities, liberties, customs, and privileges, and, insofar as possible, to restore them and pursue them with gracious and kind favor. But if this time you are unwilling to comply with and consent to our wishes, then by every means we can we shall strive to bring you under our authority; after that it may be difficult for you to obtain or enjoy our favor. Given near Ostróda on Thursday, the day after the Division of the Apostles, in 1410. By the report of lord Nicholas, Vice-Chancellor of the Kingdom of Poland.

V. Year 1410. The King of Poland invites the citizens of Tuchola and Chojnice to join his side.

Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen, etc., to the noble and prudent landholders and citizens of Tuchola and Chojnice: grace and every good thing. Prudent and noble men, we have learned that at the urging of our enemies you withdrew from the allegiance sworn to us, and now wish to return to us if we show you favor. Let your whole community know that we wish to be gracious and kind to all who wish to return to us and to the allegiance sworn to us and faithfully adhere to us; we have decided to forgive their offense and take no vengeance upon them or their property. The only condition is this: as proof of your renewed fidelity, you must take into custody all the guests of the Cross-bearers and Bohemians who are staying in your city and on your estates, and faithfully preserve and hold them and the city on our behalf until we send our men to you. Otherwise, if you do differently, you must not blame us for whatever happens to you; you yourselves and your descendants will be the cause of it. Given at Inowrocław on Monday before the feast of Saint Hedwig, in the year etc. 10. By the report of lord Konrad von Frankenberg.

VI. Year 1410. Władysław, König von Polen, complains to Commander Heinrich von Plauen about the Order’s cruelty toward Polish prisoners.

To the venerable and noble Heinrich von Plauen, Commander at Świecie and deputy of the Hochmeister of the Teutonic Order in Prussia. Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen and Lithuania, Supreme Prince and heir of Rus’, etc. Venerable and noble lord, we have received your letters in full. In them you write to our Majesty asking that we release on parole the prisoners whom our courtiers captured in the battle on the day after Saint Dionysius, offering security that you will release our men whom your men captured as prisoners on an equal pledge or promise. Know that, moved both by your requests and by the consideration of the praiseworthy Christian custom usually observed in wars, we have released on parole all and each of the prisoners whom we captured in that battle and in the previous battle, and have set a certain day and term for them to appear before us. But the Commanders and other brothers of your Order whom our men brought to us from that battle, about whom you wrote to us, before we received your letter—because of the cruel savagery committed by your men against our people whom you took as prisoners—you led them to your castles. Who has ever heard, from the beginning of time, of Christian prisoners being tortured with such inhumanity as you presume to inflict upon your own men whom you hold as prisoners, condemning them to death by the cruel sword and other kinds of punishment, abusing Christian piety? Yet you know that we hold many more of your men as prisoners than you hold of ours, and we would wish to exercise no tyranny or impiety toward them, if your example did not lead us to do so. Indeed, because you began to exercise tyranny over our men, something we had never contemplated, we are compelled to do the same to yours. Therefore we request and exhort you, in order to obtain what we desire, to release all our men whom you hold captive, by equal exchange, just as we have released yours. Even when you held lesser office, you always hated the shedding of human blood. Now, though you have greater power to prevent it, you have allowed our captive men to be put to the sword, as if intending that we pursue yours with equal punishment. We shall indeed be compelled to do so if you continue to observe so detestable a custom. Moreover, you write that you wish to exchange Jarosław, standard-bearer of Poznań, whom you captured as a prisoner in a certain skirmish near Złotów, for the Vogt of the New March whom we hold prisoner. Know, therefore, that Jarosław was fully restored to liberty by the man who captured him in that skirmish, released from his parole, and let go; he is not bound to anyone in captivity or by a pledge. Given on Saint Crispin’s day, in the year of our Lord 1410. Send us a reply to these matters by the present messenger. By the report of Donyn, canon of the churches of Sandomierz and Kruszwica, protonotary of our court.

VII. Year 1410. The King of Poland shows the dukes, counts, barons, and others who assisted the Order at Tuchola the injuries he suffered at the hands of the Order.

Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen and Lithuania, Supreme Prince and heir of Rus’, etc., to all and each of the princes, counts, barons, knights, nobles, retainers, and others, wherever they are residing at Tuchola or elsewhere, who came to render aid to the Cross-bearers of Prussia and their Order: greetings, and an invitation to recognize the truth of justice. Illustrious, magnificent, noble, and famous men, we cannot fully understand why, though endowed with many marks of probity and virtue and supported by due reason, you came to the aid of the Cross-bearers against us without knowing our just cause, which, by the Lord’s granting, we shall establish. They had perpetual peace treaties with us and our Kingdom of Poland, confirmed by apostolic and imperial letters and by letters of us, our predecessors, and their Order; nevertheless, disregarding their own safety and prodigal of their honor, they hostilely invaded our lands of Dobrzyń, Nakło, and others, and turned them to ashes by fire and sword. They caused immeasurable damage and loss and threw down in ruins certain castles there, erected and built at great expense and with heavy labor, to the disgrace and contempt of our royal Majesty. Despite these and other injuries that we have often suffered from them, although we repeatedly requested them, they would not answer us. Whenever we wished to bring these injuries to the knowledge of you and other princes who profess the Christian faith, they always blocked our messengers from traveling and sought to capture or kill them, so that our justice remained unknown to you and the other Christian princes. If it had reached your ears, perhaps they would have received no aid from you, nor could their gold and silver have bent you to support them; rather, you would have inclined to justice instead of their inducements and payment. By God’s grant, we believe that we possess that justice. To establish it more fully, and so that you may learn that the aforesaid Cross-bearers had no cause to wage war against us, send to us two of your noble men, to whom we shall demonstrate the purity of our innocence and justice, under our safe and Christian conduct; or we shall send two of our nobles to you to explain our justice, provided that you grant them full security and freedom to come to you and depart from you. Given at Inowrocław on the Sunday immediately before the feast of Saint Martin, in the year 1410. We ask you to send us a reply concerning these matters. By the report of Donyn, protonotary.

VIII. Year 1410. Władysław (Jagiełło), King of Poland, concludes a truce with Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister.

Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen, Prince of Lithuania and heir of Rus’, etc., makes known to all by this letter that, on the eve of the recent feast of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, our councillors and those of the magnificent and venerable lord Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister of the Order of the Teutonic Brothers of the Blessed Mary, etc., having duly agreed on a term for settling the wars, lawsuits, disputes, controversies, and losses of battle that have so disastrously arisen up to now between us and our Kingdom and Crown on one side, and the aforesaid Order on the other; and concerning our Kingdom and Crown of Poland, and the lands, duchies, possessions, dominions, and all other territories, whether Catholic or schismatic, or subject to their authority, and all their allies, people, and subjects of whatever status, condition, rank, or eminence, especially the illustrious and magnificent princes, our dearest brothers, Alexander, also called Vytautas, Herzog von Litauen; Bogusław of Słupsk; and the brothers Jan and Siemowit, Dukes of Masovia, with their allies, people, subjects, lands, duchies, provinces, dominions, and possessions, whether Catholic, schismatic, or pagan, of whatever status, condition, language, or rank, and however they hold them, by whatever title or terms; and, on the other side, the same lord Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister, and his aforesaid Order, lands, allies, and all people subject to them, have duly and actually made, arranged, established, and sanctioned true and perfect Christian peace and truce, to be held firmly and effectively without any pretence or color of deceit, for four consecutive weeks beginning on the coming Sunday, under the conditions set out below.

First, the Hochmeister and his Order shall preserve during this truce all castles and cities—namely Strasburg, Reddin, Toruń, Nieszawa, and Bylaw—and the people living in or belonging to them, whose possession in the lands of Prussia we have held until now. He shall give full and complete freedom to the people and persons in them to travel around, go, ride, transport and lead goods, forage, and freely perform every act throughout his lands, cities, and places, and to provision, supply, repair, and maintain those castles and cities, except that the Castle of Toruń itself and the people in it are included in this truce. During the interval, provisions may be brought to it from the city and from elsewhere, but it must not be stocked or strengthened with any greater supply of food, drink, firewood, defenses, weapons, troops, fortifications, or protection than is there now; when the truce expires, the same stores and defenses must remain there in the same number, weight, and quantity as now, and no more, under pledge of faith, conscience, and honor. It is also expressly agreed that we and our people shall hold peacefully and quietly during the truce the Castle of Toruń, its castle precinct and the mill situated beneath it, and everything else contained within the castle enclosure. The lord Hochmeister shall meanwhile not restore, repair, or rebuild the Lubicz mill, either himself or through another, in any way. It is also specifically and expressly agreed that the men and household of our Castle of Toruń shall have full and complete freedom to go from the castle to the city, from the city to the castle, and outside the city of Toruń to any places they choose, along the old, usual, and customary roads and paths, and there to travel, ride, transport goods, converse with people, and carry on every activity. The lord Hochmeister and all his men shall meanwhile make or prepare no new buildings, structures, or equipment useful for assaulting that castle; they shall keep such equipment in the same number, strength, and quantity as it is now until the truce expires. We and our men shall have, hold, enjoy, and peacefully possess the aforesaid castles and cities, with their uses, boundaries, and appurtenances, during the truce as stated above.

If any men belonging to the Hochmeister, of whatever status or condition, happen to raise disputes or quarrels against any of our people in our lands, cities, or places, or commit violence or injuries, inflict wounds, or perpetrate any serious excess, nevertheless the aforesaid truce shall remain inviolable and unharmed. Neither we nor our officials shall exact vengeance or punishment from such men; rather, they must report the matter to the Hochmeister and his officials so that justice may be done. We decree that all prisoners from both sides, whether already ransomed or yet to be ransomed—except princes and prisoners who are held in remote parts and could not timely come to the appointed term to present themselves in captivity or pay the due amount of their ransom—shall have a period of one week after this truce expires to present themselves as prisoners or pay their ransom. Those for whom that term is unsuitable shall meet the other term assigned to them.

We, together with our councillors listed below, approve, ratify, confirm, and by this letter establish as binding these truces of peace, arranged and made between us in the praiseworthy, lawful, and reasonable manner described: the reverend father in Christ, lord Jakub, Bischof von Płock; the magnificent men Sandziwóg of Ostroróg, Palatin zu Poznań; Jakub of Koniecpole, Palatin zu Sieradz; Maciej of Łabiszyn, Palatine of Brześć Kujawski; Piotr Szafraniec, sub-chamberlain of Kraków; Mikołaj, Judge of Poznań; Jan, Castellan of Łęczyca; Jurman, Castellan of Międzyrzecz; Cotton, Kastellan zu Nakło; Mikołaj of Oporów, cupbearer; the hunter of Łęczyca; Bartosz, Captain of Sieradz; Womarathon, Castellan of Bejsce; and Piotr Miedźwiecki, Marshal of our court. Together and separately, each on his own behalf, we accept them as ratified, approved, and firm, and confirm them by this letter, decreeing that they shall have lasting force. On our faith, souls, conscience, and honor, and on our word, we promise to observe them firmly and inviolably, without opposing them by word, deed, or action, and with every deceit and fraud removed. If, God forbid, we in any way inflict damage upon the lands, duchies, provinces, districts, people, or subjects of the aforesaid Hochmeister and his allies, we promise and undertake in good faith to make full and complete restitution. If we ourselves, or anyone acting through us or another, directly or indirectly, explicitly or implicitly, secretly or publicly, openly or covertly, should attempt anything contrary to the foregoing or any part of it—by word, deed, action, gesture, sign, or any other indication—thereby impeding this peace truce, may that bring disgrace upon our faith, soul, conscience, and honor; may we be deemed infamous, without glory, and faithless, deprived of honor and subject forever to shame, as transgressors against the faith, conscience, and honor pledged above. We submit ourselves to the admonition, exhortation, and commands of any subject of Prussia or anyone else who possesses or holds this letter. We exclude all foreign or extraneous glosses, explanations, interpretations, or additions concerning the foregoing or any part of it; we wish this letter to be interpreted and explained according to the plain meaning of its own terms. In witness of this letter our seals and those of our aforesaid councillors are attached. Given at our castle of Nieszawa on Tuesday, the day after the Conception of the glorious Virgin Mary, in the year of our Lord 1410.

Original letter of the four-week truce of peace, dated at Nieszawa on the day after the Conception of the glorious Virgin Mary.

IX. Year 1410. The King of Poland congratulates Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister, on attaining this highest dignity in the Order.

To the magnificent and venerable lord Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister of the Order of the German House in Prussia. Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen, etc. Magnificent and venerable lord, your sincerity may know that we have always taken pleasure in your advancement, and we congratulate you with singular affection that the height of the Lord’s counsel has raised you to so distinguished a summit of dignity; we choose you above others to possess this dignity. For until now, in times of peace, mutual zeal of charity has flourished between us, and we expect it to flourish still, with the grace of the Holy Spirit’s help, provided that you do not adopt the arrogant conduct that your predecessors showed toward our Majesty in their injustice. Then the losses of war and the incitements of hatred that have so miserably endured between us until now could easily be put to rest and cease; they have always been hateful to us. But who stirred them up is known to Him from whom nothing is hidden, whose judgment examines the purity of conscience. Since the desire and purpose of both of us, as well as our own, has always been to stifle the storms of battle, lest the Christian faith be assailed by such hardships and instead enjoy the sweetness of peace, we invite you to come to us at Raciąż, according to the decision of the councillors on both sides, to discuss matters concerning our agreements. Given at Brześć on Tuesday, the day after the Conception of the Blessed Mary, in the year of our Lord 1410. The King in person.

Diplomatic acts during the reign of Władysław Jagiełło, for the year 1411.

I. Year 1411. Władysław, König von Polen, and Vytautas, Grand Duke, promise the Order that they will observe the truce for two further days, during which they will negotiate the conclusion of a treaty.

We, Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen and Lithuania, Supreme Prince and heir of Rus’, etc., together with the illustrious prince lord Alexander, also called Vytautas, Herzog von Litauen, our dearest brother, and the valiant and noble men Sandziwóg of Ostroróg, Palatin zu Poznań; Nicholas of Michałów, Palatin zu Sandomierz; Jan of Chełmce, Palatin zu Kalisz; and Krystyn of Koziegłowy, Castellan of Sieradz, jointly and severally, all as one, on behalf of ourselves and of all other people of whatever status or condition, pledge by this letter, on our faith and honor and by the force of our oath, that the peace truce arranged and confirmed between us, our Crown and Kingdom on one side, and the venerable Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister, and his Order on the other, which has been observed for the two immediately preceding days—that is, from Saint Vincent the Martyr’s day, which was Thursday, through the following Friday up to midnight inclusive, as is clearly set out in letters made and sealed on both sides, with certain articles, points, and clauses expressed in attached or interleaved schedules—we wish and are bound to observe inviolably, without any deceit or fraud, for two consecutive days immediately following the date of this letter, until sunrise on the next Monday or until such time as the sun could rise when the mists clear. During this peace truce, under safe-conduct, we shall send our aforesaid brother, the illustrious prince Alexander, also called Vytautas, Herzog von Litauen, with six other of our councillors and envoys, whom we sent on the recent Thursday and Friday to negotiate a union of peace on the island at the mouth of the Vistula outside the city of Toruń, accompanied by a suitable retinue of horses and men, to a place to be assigned to them. There they shall negotiate with the reverend father in Christ, lord Johann, Bishop of Würzburg; Konrad von Wittinghoff, Commander of Livonia; and the noble Heinrich von Plauen the Elder, whom the same Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister, has expressly appointed in his letters for this purpose, concerning the means, ways, and terms by which a path to peace, union, and concord may be reached. We do not wish the days of the aforesaid peace truce to be impaired or cease on that account, should it happen (which God forbid) that any dispute, war, contention, or disagreement arise among the people of either party or anyone else, by word, deed, or action. Rather, this peace truce is to remain inviolable and retain its strength and firmness. If we, or anyone else, should attempt anything by word, deed, or action contrary to our promises, whereby this peace truce might appear to be impaired, may that turn to the disgrace of our fame, faith, and honor. In witness of this letter our seals are attached. Given at our camp near Raciąż, on Saturday, the eve of the Conversion of Saint Paul, in the year of our Lord 1411.

II. Year 1411. Polish nobles seek peace with the Teutonic Order.

We, lord Tomasz Tanefeld, lord Grzymal Neynowski, lord Kuncze Rydeburg, Nickel von Redern, Johann von Redern, Schisko von Cakamnisch, Hans Mosschen, Heinrich Haugwitz, Nickel Rote, Kuncze Weyderaw, Barthisch Mentczisch, Dominik Kostrollski, Steffani Restoffski, Nicolay Glynski, Nickel Bosser, Jurg Barnth, Jacob Krafgaski, Endres Zeploski, Otto Danefeld, Heinrich Baruth, Dyman Schuska, Jorg Falkenberg, Kirstan, Stanike, Wenzlaff, Johann Hincz Jerikey, Heinrich Glaubiss, Boydiky Sterneglicz, Dyrski Stamspi, Boydiky Samboski, knights and squires, make public acknowledgment in this letter to all who see, hear, or read it. We were attacked and injured at Reszel while under the safe-conduct of the venerable, mighty lord brother Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister of the Teutonic Order; afterward, the most illustrious prince lord Władysław, König von Polen, etc., our gracious lord, fully informed us of all the disputes that had occurred during this war with the aforesaid lord Hochmeister. In particular, one article in the letter of agreement states that all violations of peace and safe-conduct committed on both sides in this war are to be set aside without deceit. Therefore we waive the safe-conduct that the aforesaid Hochmeister, the noble lord Heinrich the Elder of Plauen, the Commander of Elbląg, and the Commander of Ostróda gave us under their seals. We pledge and promise under our faith and honor, in word and deed, together with our helpers and servants, never to do anything that might cause harm, without evasion, to the aforesaid lord Hochmeister, lord Heinrich von Plauen the Elder, the Commanders of Elbląg and Ostróda, or those involved with them. We likewise pledge on behalf of Sigemund Rothe, who was not present when this letter was written, that he shall keep firm and steadfast all points and articles expressed in this letter and shall not act contrary to them. In witness of this, we, the aforesaid lord Tomasz Tanefeld, lord Grzymal Neynowski, lord Kuncze Rydeburg, Nickel von Redern, Schisko von Cakamnisch, Heinrich Haugwitz, Nickel Rote, Barthisch Mentczisch, Dominik Kostrollski, Jacob Krafgaski, and Jorg Falkenberg, have caused our seals to be attached to this present letter, given at Elbląg on the Friday before Saint Valentine’s day, in the year 1411.

III. Year 1411. Peace between the King of Poland and the Order, by which the lands of Michałów and Chełmno remain with the Order.

Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen, lord of the lands of Kraków, Sandomierz, Sieradz, Łęczyca, and Kuyavia, Supreme Prince of Lithuania, lord and heir of Pomerania and Rus’, together with the illustrious prince lord Alexander, also called Vytautas, Herzog von Litauen, etc., our dearest brother, makes known by this letter to all whom it concerns that, moved by pious compassion and salutary reflection, and considering in our mind how many and great evils result from the disturbance of wars and disagreements, how many dangers to souls arise from disputes, and how much Christian blood is shed in battles, we wish to render a special service to our Creator. We have therefore resolved to withdraw from the wars and the many acts of hostility that have arisen between us, our Kingdom, and the lands of Lithuania and our other territories on one side, and the Hochmeister of the Order of the Hospital of the Blessed Mary of the Teutonic House of Jerusalem, his Order, and its lands in Prussia and Livonia and all other lands subject to it on the other, despite the grave losses they have caused. Desiring to restore to a peaceful and tranquil state what the losses of disputes have destroyed, we have made with the same Hochmeister, his Order, and their lands a union of perpetual peace and an inviolable treaty, which we promise to maintain and observe on our faith and honor, without deceit or fraud. We have included in this union all our allies, of every status and condition and wherever they reside, particularly these princes: lords Jan and Siemowit, Dukes of Masovia, their children and heirs; and Bogusław, Herzog von Słupsk, etc., our dearest brothers. We do not wish them to be separated from the bond of this union. So that this union, conceived with such mature and careful deliberation, may be brought to a lasting and firm order and perpetually observed, we have resolved to regulate it wholly by the articles set out below.

First and principal article: all disputes, controversies, and injuries between us, our Kingdom of Poland, our lands of Lithuania, and all our other allies and subjects on one side, and the aforesaid Hochmeister, Order, lands, and subjects on the other, shall be abandoned and entirely laid to rest.

All prisoners captured in this war on either side shall be freed and released from captivity without deceit. All ransoms and exactions of prisoners not yet collected shall be cancelled and reduced to nothing; if any sureties or written bonds have been given for their ransom, all shall be voided, and the guarantors shall be free, without any deceit or fraud.

All castles and towns acquired by either side in these wars shall be restored to each rightful party without deceit, and both spiritual and secular persons shall be released from the oaths of allegiance and homage they gave to either side; letters to this effect shall be issued to them. Upon surrender, the castles and towns are not to be laid waste or damaged; their castellans and captains shall receive all defenses of the castles and their own property and may take them away without hindrance.

The land of the Samogitians is excepted: we, lords Władysław, König von Polen, and Alexander, also called Vytautas, Herzog von Litauen, shall hold it peacefully and quietly in possession for the lifetimes of both of us, unless we freely choose to yield it to the Order before our deaths. This shall be confirmed by open letters. After our deaths, the Order may take possession of that land without hindrance, with all rights and properties, according to the terms of the letters previously granted to the Order concerning its appropriation.

Siemowit, Herzog of Masovia shall freely hold the small land and district of Zawkrze, which he had formerly pledged to the Order; once the sum for which that land was pledged is released, he shall be discharged and acquitted.

The land of Dobrzyń shall remain with the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland, along with all lands that the Crown of Poland held in possession before this war. The lands of Pomerania, Michałów, and Chełmno, and Nieszawa, Moryń, and Orłowo with their appurtenances, shall remain with the Order, as shall all other lands that the Order held in possession before this war.

The permanent holdings of the castles of Drezdenko and Santok shall be submitted to the decision of twelve worthy men, to be chosen by the Hochmeister and us when the aforesaid Master is requested by us. If they cannot bring the matter to a conclusion, it shall then be referred to the supreme arbitrator, the lord Pope. The same shall be done concerning all boundaries of the Kingdom of Poland and the lands of Lithuania, etc. Likewise, matters concerning the boundaries of the Dukes of Masovia and Pomerania shall be submitted to the decision of twelve worthy men chosen by us and the Hochmeister.

All properties of the churches of Gniezno, Wrocław, and others lying under the protection of the Order, and in its lands, shall be preserved according to their rights and shall not be alienated unless the prelates freely consent. The same shall be done with the Order’s bishops’ properties held under the Crown: they shall remain according to their rights and not be alienated without the prelates’ consent. Any violations of peace or safe-conducts committed by either side in this war shall be laid to rest without deceit. Merchants of both parties shall be able to travel with their goods without hindrance through lands and waters, according to the ancient custom.

To the end that perpetual friendship may endure between the Kingdom of Poland, Lithuania and all lands subject to them, and the Order and all lands subject to it, and that the union of perpetual treaty may not be violated by any disagreements, whenever disagreements or impediments arise, each side shall appoint six persons; those twelve persons shall have full authority to settle the same disputes, disturbances, and impediments by legal means and friendly agreement. If they cannot agree fully, they shall refer the matters to the supreme arbitrator, the lord Pope, and this procedure shall be observed for all time. Any cases that arise concerning inheritance, ownership, fiefs, or debts shall be tried and settled in the court of the district where they lie. Whatever concerns feudal property shall be settled under the lord of the fief according to the law customarily observed there.

We shall require all unbelievers living in our lands to accept the Christian faith; to extend the faith, churches shall be built and priests placed in them, and all pagan errors uprooted. Likewise, the Hochmeister and Order shall be bound to convert the unbelievers in Prussia and Livonia and make them maintain the faith. Both parties shall notify the unbelievers in neighboring lands of this union and settlement, exhorting them to accept the Christian faith. If they refuse, the parties shall then aid one another to convert them to the Christian faith. If both parties agree to march there with their armies, then in all matters and difficulties, especially the division of lands they may subdue, they shall observe and maintain what is set out in their earlier letters, unless the aforesaid parties voluntarily decree otherwise.

All fugitives in this war, spiritual and secular, on both sides may return without hindrance to their own property and possess it as they possessed it before; they shall receive the favor and grace of their lords as before. The sole exception is the lord Bishop of Warmia, who shall have safe-conduct to return to his bishopric. The Hochmeister and Order shall do him no violence, but only what they may lawfully do.

König Sigismund of Hungary shall be included in this settlement and peace if he wishes, without deceit. The Hochmeister shall promptly inform him of the terms of this union and let us know the will of the same König von Ungarn. Meanwhile, we shall not damage the König von Ungarn or wage war against him if he does not hinder us. But if he wishes to hinder us or wage war against us, we shall be able to repay him in kind and defend ourselves with all our strength against his attacks.

Both parties shall also continue to enjoy all their privileges, letters, praiseworthy customs, and rights as they have existed until now, without any derogation from the articles settled here. Moreover, the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland, together with the lands and people of Lithuania, shall never for all time act against the Order or join its enemies. Likewise, the Hochmeister and Order shall never for all time act against the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland and the lands of Lithuania and their subjects, nor join the enemies of the Crown and the lands of Lithuania, without fraud or deceit.

In witness and fuller confirmation, the seals of our Majesty are attached together with those of the prelates: Nicholas, by God’s grace Archbishop of the church of Gniezno; Piotr, Bischof zu Kraków; and Albert, Bischof zu Poznań; and of the princes, Jan and Siemowit, Dukes of Masovia; Simeon, also called Lingwen, brother of Sigismund, brother of Vytautas, Herzog; Simeon’s son Jamunt of Lithuania; the dukes; and of the barons, namely the Castellans of Kraków; Sandziwóg of Poznań; Maciej of Kalisz; Nicholas of Sandomierz; Jakub of Sieradz; Czesław of Brześć; Maciej of Włocławek; the Palatines; Michał of Sandomierz; Jan of Kalisz; Nicholas of Santok; the Castellans; Zbigniew, Marschall of the Kingdom of Poland; Piotr Szafraniec, sub-chamberlain of Kraków; Nicholas of Czarnków, Judge of Poznań; Albert, also called Moniwid, Captain of Vilnius; Stanisław, also called Czupurna, Marshal of the land of Lithuania; Gedigold, formerly Voivode of Kyiv; Krystyn, also called Ościk; Radziwiłł; Rampold; Sunyglon; and Jan Nemer, also barons of Lithuania; and the cities of Kraków, Sandomierz, Poznań, Kalisz, Brześć, and Włocławek. Done at Toruń on Sunday, the eve of the Purification of the glorious Virgin Mary, in the year of our Lord 1411, in the presence of the valiant men Sandziwóg of Ostroróg, Palatin zu Poznań; Nicholas of Michałów, Palatin zu Sandomierz; Jan of Chełmce, Palatin zu Kalisz; Nicholas of Błociszewo, Kastellan zu Santok; Zbigniew, Marschall of the Kingdom of Poland; Piotr Szafraniec, sub-chamberlain of Kraków; and Nicholas of Czarnków, Judge of Poznań, whose names are written above, and many other faithful and trustworthy men. Given by the hand of the reverend father in Christ, lord Nicholas, by God’s grace Archbishop of the church of Kalisz, Vice-Chancellor of the Kingdom of Poland.

And I, Johannes, formerly Johannes Rosener of Sorau, cleric of the Diocese of Meissen, public notary by imperial authority, was present together with my colleague, the public notary Balthasar, and the aforesaid witnesses at the presentation and receipt of the aforesaid letters, the insertion of the decree, and all the other matters set out above, while they were being done and carried out as stated. I saw and heard them done. Therefore, at the command of the aforesaid reverend father in Christ, the Bishop, and at the request of the aforesaid procurator, I faithfully transcribed this present public instrument, carefully collated it with my aforesaid colleague, and wrote it in my own hand in this public form; I authenticated it with my usual sign and name, together with the attachment of the aforesaid Bishop’s smaller seal, in faith and testimony of all the foregoing, upon request. I, the notary, certify that the clause concerning the people residing in the districts of those castles, who are not to be despoiled, omitted in the twenty-eighth line from the bottom after the word “laid waste,” is marked with this sign, and was omitted through inadvertence, not by fault.

IV. Year 1411. Treaty made between the King of Poland and Vytautas and the Order (translated from Latin into German).

We, Władysław, by God’s grace King of Poland, Supreme Prince of Lithuania and heir of Rus’, etc., together with the illustrious prince Alexander, also called Vytautas, Herzog von Litauen, etc., our dearest brother, make known by this letter to all that, considering with compassionate reflection and benevolent intent, and taking to heart in pious thought how many and great harms arise from violent discord and strife, how many dangers to souls come from wars, and how much Christian blood is shed in battle, we have resolved to render a special and worthy service to God our Creator. We therefore set our minds to withdraw from the practice of the aforesaid wars and hostilities, which have arisen with great hardship between us, our Kingdom of Poland, the lands of Lithuania and our other lands on one side, and the spiritual lord Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister of the Teutonic Order in Prussia, etc., his Order and its lands on the other.
