We wish to restore to a peaceful and secure condition the common good that has been destroyed and broken by the injustices of discord. We have made with the same Hochmeister and his Order an agreement of perpetual peace and an inviolable covenant, which we pledge on our honor and faith to maintain without deceit or evasion. In this agreement we wish to include and embrace all and each of our helpers, whatever their station or condition and in whatever lands they dwell or reside, especially these princes and lords: Jan and Siemowit, Dukes of Masovia, their children and heirs, and Bogusław, Herzog von Słupsk, etc., our dearest brothers; we do not wish them to be excluded from the bond of this agreement. So that the agreement, conceived with mature and careful consideration, may be brought to a firm and lasting order, we have set it out in the following articles and pledge to confirm it without deceit, securing it by the seal of our Majesty on this letter.

First and principal article: all hostilities, ill-will, disputes, and injuries between us, our Kingdom of Poland, our lands of Lithuania and our other lands, our helpers and subjects on one side, and the aforesaid Hochmeister, his Order, lands, and subjects on the other, shall be forgiven and entirely laid to rest. All prisoners on both sides shall be free and released without deceit. All unpaid ransoms shall be cancelled; if any prisoner has given sureties or written bonds for ransom, they too shall be void, and the guarantors shall be free, without deceit or evasion.

All castles, houses, cities, and lands gained by either side during this war shall be restored to each party without deceit. All people, spiritual and secular, shall be released from the oaths and obligations of allegiance they swore to either side, and letters shall be issued to this effect. In surrendering these castles and cities, their buildings and other structures shall not be damaged or destroyed; the people belonging to them shall not be robbed or harmed. Their captains shall take all defenses and their own belongings with them and carry them home without hindrance.

The land of Samogitia is excepted: the King and Vytautas, Herzog shall hold it in peaceful possession for both their lifetimes, unless they freely wish to yield and give it to the Order before their deaths. This shall be confirmed by open letters, so that after their deaths the Order may take possession of the land without hindrance, with all rights and properties, according to the letters previously granted to the Order concerning its acquisition. Siemowit, Herzog shall freely keep the land of Zawkrze, which he had formerly pledged to the Order, and shall be released and acquitted of the money for which he pledged it. The land of Dobrzyń shall remain with the Crown. All other lands that the Crown possessed before the war, and the lands of Pomerania, Michałów, and Chełmno, Nieszawa, Moryń, and Orłowo with their appurtenances, shall remain with the Order, as shall all other lands that the Order possessed before the war.

The question of possession of Drezdenko and Santok shall be referred to the decision of twelve honorable persons chosen by the King and the Hochmeister when the Hochmeister is requested by the King. If those twelve cannot conclude the matter, they shall submit it to our lord the Pope as arbitrator. The same shall be done concerning all boundaries of the Kingdom and the lands of Lithuania, etc. Likewise, the disputes over the boundaries of the Dukes of Masovia and Słupsk shall be referred to the decision and settlement of twelve persons; if they cannot decide them, they shall be submitted to our lord the Pope as arbitrator. Disputes concerning certain islands near Gołyń, fisheries, ships, and riverbanks of the Vistula and Drwęca shall likewise be referred to the decision and settlement of twelve men.

All properties of the churches of Gniezno, Włocławek, and others lying under the protection of the Order and in its lands shall be preserved according to their rights and not alienated except by the free will of the prelates. The same shall apply to properties of bishops of the Order that they hold under the Crown: these shall remain according to their rights and not be alienated without the prelates’ consent. Violations of peace, security, or safe-conduct committed by either side in this war shall be set aside and resolved without deceit. Merchants of both parties shall travel and pass with all their goods, without hindrance, over land and water according to ancient custom.

So that perpetual friendship may remain between the Kingdom of Poland, Lithuania and all their subject lands on one side, and the Order and all its subject lands on the other, and so that this agreement of perpetual peace may not be disturbed by any discord, if any dispute or conflict arises between them, each side shall appoint six persons. These twelve persons shall have full authority to settle the disputes, conflicts, and obstacles by law or friendly agreement. If they cannot agree in their judgment, they shall send the matters to our Holy Father the Pope as arbitrator, and this shall be observed for ever. If any matters arise concerning inheritance, ownership, land, property, or debt, these shall be settled and judged in the court of the district where they lie. Matters concerning fiefs shall be concluded according to the customary law in the court of the lord of the fief.

The King and Vytautas, Herzog shall require all unbelievers in their lands to adopt the Christian faith; to extend the faith, churches shall be built and priests placed in them, and all pagan errors uprooted and driven out. Likewise, the Hochmeister and Order shall convert all unbelievers in Prussia and Livonia to the faith. Both parties shall make this agreement known to the neighboring unbelieving lands and exhort them to accept the Christian faith. If they refuse, both parties shall help one another to convert them. If both parties agree to march together with their armies, in all their affairs and difficulties, and especially in dividing the lands they subdue, they shall abide by what is set out in their earlier letters, unless both parties freely decide otherwise.

All fugitives in this war, spiritual and secular, on both sides may return without hindrance to possess their goods as they held them before, and shall have their lords’ favor and grace as formerly. The sole exception is the lord Bishop of Warmia, who shall have safe-conduct to return to his bishopric; the Hochmeister shall do him no violence, but only what he may do lawfully. If he wishes, König Sigismund of Hungary shall be included in this settlement and peace. The Hochmeister shall promptly inform him of its terms and assure him that, meanwhile, the King of Poland will do no harm to or wage war against the König von Ungarn so long as the latter does not hinder him. If the König von Ungarn should hinder him or wage war against him, the King of Poland may repay him in kind and defend himself with all his strength.

Both parties shall retain their letters, privileges, praiseworthy customs, and rights as before, provided that none of them derogates from the articles expressly settled here. For all time, the Crown of Poland, together with the lands and people of Lithuania, shall never act against the Order or join its enemies. Likewise, the Hochmeister and Order shall never act against the Crown of Poland and the lands of Lithuania or join their enemies, without deceit or evasion.

In fuller confirmation of all the foregoing, we have caused this letter to be secured with the hanging seals of our two Majesties and of the princes, prelates, counts, and cities named below: first, Jan and Siemowit of Masovia; Simeon, also called Lingwen, brother of Sigismund; and Simeon’s son Janumcy of Lithuania; Nicholas, Erzbischof zu Gniezno; Piotr of Kraków and Albert of Poznań, bishops; Krystyn, Burggraf of Kraków; Sandziwóg of Poznań; Jakub of Sieradz; Czesław of Brześć; Maciej of Włocławek, voivodes; Michał of Sandomierz and Jan of Kalisz, castellans; Zbigniew, Marschall of the Kingdom of Poland; Piotr Szafraniec, sub-chamberlain of Kraków; Nicholas, Burggraf of Santok; Nicholas of Czarnków, Judge of Poznań; Albert, also called Moniwid, Captain of Vilnius; Stanisław, also called Supornaw, Marshal of Lithuania; Gedigold, also called Voivode of Kyiv; Krystyn, also called Ościk; Radziwiłł; Rumbald; Simeon Gailon; Jan Nemür, counts of Lithuania; and the cities of Kraków, Sandomierz, Poznań, Kalisz, Brześć, and Włocławek. Given at Toruń on the eve of the Purification of the honored Virgin Mary, in the year of the Lord 1411.

V. Year 1411. The King of Poland complains about the Hochmeister. The Hochmeister’s answer follows.

Thus the King of Poland wrote to the Master: Venerable and religious friend, sincerely beloved by us: from the time our acquaintance began, we had such confidence in you that we expected the sincerity formed between us to endure continually. For that reason we had a special consolation that greatly refreshed our heart when sweet and heartening news of your promotion to the office of Hochmeister reached us. On hearing of your promotion, we immediately began to hope that the wars your predecessors and your Order had stirred up against us would be settled and entirely brought to an end. We hoped for nothing else than that, from gratitude for our acquaintance and from the benefits of the agreement made between us and your Order, great advantages for the expansion of the orthodox faith would follow. We strove to strengthen this agreement more firmly and repeatedly informed you through our distinguished envoys that we pledged, and still pledge, firmly to observe the perpetual union concluded with you and your Order. You too, through those same envoys, offered yourself as most willing to observe the noted covenants of perpetual peace. But we do not know why or how your sincerity changed into another disposition and wounded and frustrated the confidence in you that we had held, since under the appearance of such charitable conduct and the sweetness of such sincere professions, you sought to defame and blacken our standing before the König von Ungarn and the other Christian princes by many false accusations. Among other accusations, you did not hesitate to charge us, against God and justice, with having broken the agreements established between you, us, and your Order, although by God’s grace we have never done this. We have effectively fulfilled all our promises and, with pure intent, wish still to fulfill whatever remains to be done. But, sincere friend, consider whether you were entitled to act as described, while maintaining with us such an appearance of sincerity, and to darken an innocent man with such grave accusations. Consider also whether you have properly fulfilled your own promises and whether you have justly retained the money due to us, which you have not taken care to pay. We are now given to understand that you are preparing mercenary troops and other armed forces to begin war against us. We therefore ask you to inform us of your intentions, as is proper among Catholic men, so that we may know what to expect from you. Given at Kraków on Wednesday, the very feast of Saint Catherine, in the year of our Lord 1411. The King in person.

The following schedule was enclosed in the letter. It stated: We are further informed that certain of our subjects refuse to obey you with due submission, and indeed do not fear to oppose you; to restrain their insolence you have, it is said, summoned mercenary knights from foreign and distant lands, whose arrival will cause you and your Order great expense from your treasuries. Since we have received from you a pact of pure sincerity, we deeply regret before almighty God the losses you suffer. We are greatly astonished, however, that your sincerity, having so often experienced the purity of our friendship, has so little confidence in us, despite the losses and injuries we have borne for your sake without sparing our own interests, and from which we withdrew although there was no necessity to do so; we would not have done so for anyone else. You seek help elsewhere to subdue your rebels at great loss and heavy expense, although, had you asked us for assistance, we would have been ready to send several of our captains with armed men from Poland or Lithuania to help you without great expense and suppress the obstinacy of your rebels. We hoped that, when an opportunity arose for us, we would receive the same from you. Therefore, may your kindness inform us fully through the honorable lord Custodian of Sandomierz, protonotary of our court, whom we trust, whether any assistance from us would be useful to you; and let him also tell us any other matters you wish us to know. We have instructed him, after receiving the money, to visit your sincerity and convey what our Marshal Zbigniew was to report to you on our behalf; then you will learn with what favors we shall treat you.

The Order’s reply to the King of Poland: Most serene prince, etc. Having recently received and clearly understood the letters of Your Majesty, in which you graciously declare that since the time of our mutual acquaintance you have had great confidence in us, and that your heart was consoled when reports of our promotion to the office we now hold, unworthy though we are, reached your hearing, etc., we cannot offer sufficient thanks for such gracious favor. We implore almighty God’s mercy to make good our shortcomings and grant you his gifts a hundredfold, to confirm and strengthen in you such love toward us and our Order, and to increase it continually with fortunate progress, so that peace, charity, and sincere friendship between us may bring comfort and tranquility to the subjects of both our parties and advance the orthodox Catholic faith, as we see you desire in those same letters.

Most serene prince, in those same letters you appear, among other things, to blame us as though we had disturbed the peace established between us, because we retained money owed to you, etc. Most serene prince, we call God as witness that we committed nothing in this matter out of malice, but were driven by urgent cause and unbearable losses. We trust in God’s grace that, if an occasion for a mutual meeting should ever arise, we could explain clearly in person to Your Majesty the losses and wrongs we have suffered after the peace made between us, contrary to God and justice. Your royal goodness would surely then respond with compassion and take more effective measures to ensure that we receive equity for our injuries and that your people faithfully fulfill what they promised us. With this intention, and to avoid any mixture of deceit, we have delayed payment of the aforesaid debt and appealed to the Holy Apostolic See and the Holy Roman Empire, although we acted in good faith, hoping none of this would ever be necessary. We are always ready to obey Your Serenity firmly in these matters. Therefore, we earnestly and humbly beseech Your Majesty to graciously consider and weigh our pressing causes and losses, which we have suffered at the hands of Your Serenity and your people in league with our Order—not only before the battle and during it, but also beyond the battle, and, to our greater sorrow, after the peace was confirmed—and to have patience with us as we slowly proceed to send you hostages as sureties, and to defer this for a little while until the Apostolic See and the Empire have duly decreed whether we must satisfy you for the aforesaid debt despite such grave losses. If Your Highness will consider this delay, our most serene lord the Pope has deigned, of his own motion, to urge Your Highness with high and powerful pleas in his apostolic letters, moved by the compassion of paternal charity; he has decided to send us a copy of those letters, graciously granting us, in addition to our significant reasons, this special favor in the matter of delay.

You also ask to be informed what you should expect from us, since, as you say, you have been told that we are preparing mercenary troops and other armed forces to wage war on you, etc. It is clear to Your Serenity that all our dealings with you stand on friendly and peaceful terms. In answer to this request, we say that, unless we are compelled by some grave event to take up arms and disturb the peace—which we do not expect—we shall guard our honor and safety before Your Highness in every matter as befits Catholic conduct. We have also received reliable news that some time ago Your Serenity sent mercenary troops for certain purposes. Our friends and supporters in the Order advised us that the final purpose of that dispatch might be to bring about the total destruction of our Order, which, by his customary mercy, God will prevent. Accordingly, certain friends and supporters of ours have come to us at their own expense, and others are on their way; we trust in the Lord that we are not to blame for providing in time against unexpected blows that might otherwise have succeeded.

We also offer Your Highness the fullest thanks we can for having earlier, of your own accord, graciously offered to assist us with your troops if necessity required it against our rebellious subjects. We have regarded and still regard this as a most special favor, and we would not have been negligent in thanking you for accepting so friendly an offer, had we not been informed that Your Serenity had already sent messengers and letters to various places to obtain many men and mercenaries. When we learned this, we scarcely dared believe that your men would be available to us in our need. Given at our castle of Elbląg on the very feast of the glorious Apostle Thomas, in the year 1411.

VI. Year 1411. Władysław, König von Polen, informs the Order that he is sending his commissioners to Prussia to collect the money owed him by the Order.

Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen and Lithuania, Supreme Prince and heir of Rus’, etc., to the religious and magnificent lord Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister of the Teutonic Order of the Hospital of the Blessed Mary, his commanders, treasurers, dispensers, and the other persons appointed to pay us the money at the coming feast of Saint John the Baptist, to whom this letter may come, our sincerely beloved friends: greetings and the increase of sincere favor. We are sending to your community the valiant men Jakub of Koniecpole, Palatin zu Sieradz; Maciej of Łabiszyn, Palatine of Brześć; the Captain of Inowrocław; and the honorable Donyn, Custodian and Canon of Sandomierz, protonotary, and Piotr, Canon of Poznań, notaries of our court, our faithful and beloved men, bearers of this letter. They are fully and explicitly informed of our intentions, especially concerning the collection of the money which, as stated above, you are to pay us at the feast of Saint John the Baptist. We wish you to give them full credence in all that they report and do on our behalf on this occasion. Given at Świecie on Saturday, the eve of Pentecost, in the year of our Lord 1411, etc. The King in person.

The King of Poland’s letter of credence for collecting the money after the battle. The Iron Band.

VII. Year 1411. Letter of credence from the King of Poland, given to Nicholas Sopynski, an envoy to the Hochmeister. (The Polish heading gives the year as 1141.)

Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen and Lithuania, Supreme Prince and heir of Rus’, etc., to the venerable Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister of the Teutonic Order of the German House in Prussia, etc., our sincerely beloved friend: greetings and the increase of our desired favor. Venerable friend, sincerely beloved by us: the noble Nicholas Sopynski, informed fully and distinctly of our intentions, will come to you to report them orally on behalf of the illustrious prince lord Alexander, Duke of Lithuania, etc., our dearest brother. We ask you to give credence on this occasion to what he says on our behalf. Given at Vilnius on the very feast of the Holy Trinity, in the year of our Lord 1411. By the hand of R. Czołkonis, notary of the King’s court and of the Sandomierz chancellery.

VIII. Year 1411. The King of Poland writes to the Hochmeister that Jan Surwil is not a traitor and asks that he be allowed to sell his property in Prussia.

Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen and Lithuania, Supreme Prince and heir of Rus’, etc., to the venerable lord Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister of the Order of the German House in Prussia: greetings and the increase of our desired favor. Venerable friend, our beloved: Hans Surwil has informed us that your sincerity accuses him of treason, alleging that in former years, when disagreements and enmities between us had happily been put to rest in the sweetness of peace, he conveyed to us from every source whatever he could learn about your actions and affairs. Concerning this, we call God and our conscience to witness that we have never received from him any report of your secret decisions, nor has he revealed them to us by any sign or intelligible indication by which they could have come to our knowledge. Therefore we exhort and ask your sincerity to regard and treat him as trustworthy, free from the crime of such suspicion, honorable, and preserved in the integrity of his faith; and to grant him permission freely to sell his property that he possesses under your jurisdiction. His father’s merits require this: he pleased you and your Order in many ways, and therefore he deserves your Order’s favor rather than hatred. Given at Trakai on Tuesday within the octave of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, in the year of our Lord 1411. By the report of Piotr, Vice-Marshal.

IX. Year 1411. Letter of Pope John to the King of Poland, asking him not to burden the Order excessively over the payment of money.

John, etc., to our most beloved son in Christ, Władysław, illustrious King of Poland: health and the apostolic blessing. By reason of the apostolic office, out of paternal love we desire matters that bring peace and concord, especially for illustrious princes and powerful spiritual persons who are devoted with all humility to us and the Roman Church. We have learned how, through the action of the wickedness of the enemy of humankind, the most grievous burden of deadly war and hostility was imposed upon Your Illustriousness and our beloved sons, the Hochmeister and brothers of the German House and Hospital of Saint Mary of Jerusalem. Out of love for both parties, which we hold in our hearts, we have wished that the unspeakable harms, storms, and anxieties suffered by both sides through such discord be turned into the sweetness of peace, and for this reason we have often exhorted and urged many kings, princes, lords, spiritual and secular, of German and other lands, by messengers and letters. With their counsel, by our messengers and letters we earnestly urged Your Illustriousness to make and complete a suitable peace and concord. Your Illustriousness, now moved by Christian devotion as a Christian prince and lover of peace, graciously consented to our wish and came together with the aforesaid Hochmeister and brothers in a spirit of concord for peaceful agreement. For this we rejoice in the depths of our heart before almighty God, and we offer Your Illustriousness our most fruitful thanks.

We have learned that, among the other confirmed and recorded provisions in that peace and concord, the aforesaid Hochmeister and brothers of Your Illustriousness are bound, under specified penalties and surety, to pay you on appointed days, with prelates and nobles of your Kingdom standing as sureties for the sum of one hundred thousand Prussian marks, as is more fully stated in the letters of that obligation. We have also learned that half of this sum has already been paid to Your Illustriousness by those brothers according to the terms of the agreement, and that they are to pay the other half to you shortly, on the coming feasts of Saint Martin and the Purification of Mary. From trustworthy people we have learned that, because of the storm of the aforesaid wars, those Hochmeister, brothers, and their house have suffered such damage and diminution throughout their lands, possessions, property, and goods that they have endured great and irreparable loss and devastation in the lands, possessions, and goods by which they were known in the world to be prosperous. They have been a greater and unconquerable champion of the faith against pagan unbelief and the name of our Savior, and an unassailable wall. For this and many other great losses that they have suffered in these matters, they are unable, as we have learned from reliable reports, to pay the remaining half of that sum. Moved by paternal love, we desire to meet the brothers’ losses and misfortune by such assistance as we can and as the kindness of Your Illustriousness allows. We have particular confidence in God that Your Illustriousness, who, even when holding lesser office, received us with all the desire of your heart and continues to do so in divine love, has been and remains obedient to our wishes in all things and ways, as we have learned through various inquiries and continue to learn.

Therefore we ask with all earnestness that, for the honor of God’s name and of us and the dignity of the apostolic seat, and for the special favor and love sought by kings, princes, spiritual and secular lords of Germany and other lands, who greatly desire it, as do we from our heart, and also for the exaltation of your royal name and honor—for the throne of kings grows and is strengthened through goodness and clemency—it may please Your Majesty’s royal mercy to postpone the demand for the aforesaid half of the money, which the Hochmeister and brothers are to pay on the two stated days. This shall not prejudice the letters of obligation, the penalties, or the sureties contained in them; nor shall I or anyone else inflict any harm on the Hochmeister, the Order, their sureties, or any of their property or goods in body or possessions if payment is not made on the stated days, until we send our special envoys to Your Illustriousness to confer about the aforesaid and certain other matters concerning the Roman Church and Your Illustriousness and your lands. Our envoys will earnestly set before Your Illustriousness, with paternal affection, the matters that we hold in our heart and wish to be considered for the status and honor of your royal name. Given at Rome, etc., on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, in the second year of our pontificate.

X. Year 1411. Władysław, König von Polen, urges Albert, Graf von Schwarzburg to send some of his councillors to Kraków as hostages because of the money promised by the Hochmeister.

Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen and Lithuania, Supreme Prince and heir of Rus’, etc., to the magnificent lord Albert, Graf von Schwarzburg, our sincerely beloved friend: sincere greetings, charity, and remembrance of promises, our dearest friend. Although we doubt that this matter is in any way unknown to you, nevertheless, so that you may not claim ignorance, we have decided to inform your sincerity that the religious Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister of the German House in Prussia, together with the fellow commanders and commanders of his Order, did not pay, on the last feast of Saint Martin, the money secured by your pledges and those of the other princes, counts, and barons named in the letters concerning that money, despite having been duly and timely warned by our envoys. To this day we do not know on what grounds they entirely refuse to pay. You know how greatly you are bound and obligated to Your Highness by the promises contained in your pledges, the full wording of which has not left your memory. Therefore, on the basis of your pledge, we warn, request, and exhort your sincerity to send and dispatch two of your councillors, each with four horses, to our city of Kraków as hostages in your place, according to the promises made in your pledges. They are not to depart until we have been fully compensated for the aforesaid failure to pay at the appointed term and for the losses that followed from it. Otherwise, we shall proceed against you and anyone else whom this matter appears to concern with more severe measures of compulsion and with the actions set out in the letters of pledge. Given at Wiślica on the feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle, in the year of our Lord 1411. The King in person.

XI. Year 1411. The King of Poland complains to all princes about the Order, which, having broken the conditions of peace, is preparing for war.

To all and each of the spiritual and secular princes, counts, barons, nobles, knights, retainers, communities of cities and their governors, and all followers of the Christian religion, of whatever status, condition, or rank, to whom this letter may come: Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen and Lithuania, Supreme Prince and heir of Rus’, etc., greetings and perfect charity in the love of Christ. Most reverend fathers in Christ, illustrious princes, and renowned, noble, prudent men: we lay before you our whole devotion. We continually pour out humble prayers to our Creator that he may deign to preserve us in the desired peace and the sweetness of tranquility with the household of the faith and the followers of the Christian religion. Knowing how many troubles arise for the orthodox faith when peace is disturbed, and striving to worship the Author of peace in peace, we set aside all disturbances of war, the dangers of conflict, and the perilous losses of lawsuits. After the fullest deliberation and with great maturity, by treaties of perpetual peace we have brought to complete and perfect union, God willing, all matters of hostility and controversy that had previously arisen between us and the lords Cross-bearers of Prussia. We resolved to hold and observe that peace inviolably in every respect, and we shall effectively fulfill all our promises to the same lords Cross-bearers of Prussia. A few remain unfulfilled because of the shortness of time, but, with the Lord’s help, they will be fulfilled very soon. Their non-fulfillment has not annulled or in any way violated the peace, since no term was set for completing them; anyone who reasons about the matter can understand our injury.

We have been informed with certainty that the same lords Cross-bearers, while the firm and sincere union between us stood in place—which we hoped could be violated by no subterfuge or evasion—have erupted against us with grave and unexpected complaints, laying the blame for their own faults upon us. As has been brought to our attention, they say and claim that we have not kept our promises to them and that we are arming ourselves with pagans to destroy them. In this they wrong not so much us as our Creator, since by such accusations they stain and darken the reputation of our name, as they are accustomed to do, against justice, with matters so turbulent that they cannot enter our heart. For immediately after we made the union of perpetual peace with them, we gave back and restored to them the lands, cities, castles, dominions, and possessions that they had acquired under their control during the wars. Likewise, we freed and released from captivity all the princes, counts, barons, knights, nobles, and retainers whom we held prisoner, and fulfilled all the other provisions that could then be completed. But they refuse to recognize our actions and twist their own intentions into another form, issuing accusations against us that they have invented. Seizing an unjust pretext against us, they do not hesitate to violate the promises they made to us, for they have not paid us the money they owe at the appointed terms. Thus they strike us a double blow: first, by unjustly saying that we do not keep our agreements with them; second, by delaying payment of our own money. As we understand it, they intend to begin war with us anew, which, as almighty God is our witness, we would gladly avoid for as long as we live. Therefore we ask your sincerity not to put faith in the matters that the same lords Cross-bearers allege against us, but rather to require them to keep and observe their promises to us. Given at Kraków on the sixth day of December, in the year of our Lord 1411. By the report of lord Nicholas, Erzbischof zu Kalisz, Vice-Chancellor of the Kingdom of Poland.

XII. Year 1412. Sigismund, König der Römer, informs Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister, that he has reached certain decisions with the King of Poland at their meeting concerning the King’s affairs with the Order.

To the venerable Heinrich von Plauen, Hochmeister of the Teutonic Order, our beloved and devout friend. Sigismund, by God’s grace König der Römer, ever-august and enlarger of the Empire, and König von Ungarn, etc. Venerable, dear, devout friend: as you recently heard from the honorable brother Michel, your Order’s Kitchen Master and High Marshal, whom we hope informed you that we were to meet with the King of Poland at the recent Fastnacht, etc., we now inform you that we were together for some time and, by God’s grace, negotiated and made such a settlement as we trust will be honorable, comforting, and beneficial to the Holy Church, the Empire, the Order, and the common good. Our distinguished embassy, which we are sending without delay together with Johann, your scribe, and this present young man, shall inform you fully and precisely of it. Therefore we earnestly and diligently request that you be prepared and immediately summon your subordinates, so that when our embassy arrives it may be heard without delay and acted upon. We have sent this young man solely for this purpose and for no other. You must also ensure fully and earnestly that none of your men attack the aforesaid King and Kingdom of Poland or Vytautas, Herzog, as we fully believe and trust in you, since we have promised the same to that King. He in turn has promised us that no attack shall be made upon you or your Order by Vytautas, Herzog or his men. You should also proclaim and arrange this for Livonia and wherever else it is necessary, without delay. Given at Lubow on the Tuesday after Laetare, in the twenty-fifth year of our Kingdom of Hungary, etc., and the second year of the Roman Kingdom. By command of the lord King, Johann Kirchen.

XIII. Year 1412. Form of the oath that Władysław, König von Polen, is to swear to Sigismund, König der Römer.

We, Władysław, by the grace of God König von Polen, lord of the lands of Kraków, Sandomierz, Sieradz, Łęczyca, and Kuyavia, Supreme Prince of Lithuania, lord and heir of Pomerania and Rus’, acknowledge and declare by this letter that we are bound and obligated to the most serene prince and lord, lord Sigismund, by the same grace König der Römer, ever-august, and König von Ungarn, etc., our dearest brother, to maintain pure and perfect faith. We have been physically bound by the oath we swore after touching the wood of the life-giving Cross. We made and swore to him that oath, or sacrament of faith, in the following form of words: “I, Władysław, König von Polen, Supreme Prince of Lithuania and heir of Rus’, etc., swear that from now on I shall keep faith with my dearest brother, lord Sigismund, König der Römer, ever-august, and König von Ungarn, and shall show him sincere favor. I shall provide for the good estate and honor of him, his legitimate children, and heirs, and shall arrange his advantages and welfare everywhere. I shall never seek to obtain the good kingdoms, principalities, or dominions that he now holds or may hold in the future, nor shall I aspire or plot in any way to take or destroy his life or bring about his death. But wherever I learn, hear, or perceive anything evil or harmful concerning him, I shall faithfully warn him and assist him with all my strength against every plot of his enemies, without deceit or fraud. I shall never abandon him, his legitimate children, or his heirs; rather, for his honor and estate I shall procure, arrange, and provide his welfare and benefits as my own for as long as I live. So help me God, the holy Cross, our Holy Mary, our Christ, and all the saints.”

So that greater charity, confidence, and security may grow and increase between the aforesaid most serene princes and lords, Sigismund, König der Römer and Hungary, and Władysław, König von Polen, we, Nicholas, by God’s grace Archbishop of Kalisz, appointed to the church of Gniezno; Albert, Bishop of Pomesania; Chancellor of the Kingdom of Poland; and Zbigniew, Marschall of the Kingdom of Poland, promise and pledge that we shall keep and exhort our noble lord Władysław, König von Polen, to keep the oath he made and established to the aforesaid lord Sigismund, König der Römer and Hungary, with mature and good deliberation, in all its articles, clauses, and conditions, firmly and constantly for the whole of his life. We shall never counsel the aforesaid lord Władysław, König von Polen, our noble lord, to do anything contrary to it.

We also add that the present letter is not intended to prejudice or derogate in any way from those letters in which, after the death of either of us, a truce of five years is set out, during which justice and right concerning the lands of Rus’ and Moldavia are to be determined according to the terms of the letters made by the prelates and barons of both Kingdoms, Hungary and Poland, first at Jihlava, also called Nová Ves, and second in the Old Town. Furthermore, we, the aforesaid Władysław, König von Polen, promise that we shall have this letter sealed with our seal of Majesty when our letters have been sealed with the seal of Majesty of lord Sigismund, König der Römer and Hungary. In witness of this letter our seal, which we use, is attached together with the seals of the aforesaid venerable princes Nicholas, Erzbischof zu Kalisz appointed to Gniezno; Albert, Bischof zu Poznań; and Zbigniew, Marschall of Poland. Given at Lublin on the Wednesday immediately following the Sunday Laetare, in the year 1412.

We, the aforesaid Władysław, König von Polen, further declare that the article beginning “We also add that the present letter, etc.” has been inserted and written here in our name and in the name of our sureties, namely Archbishop Nicholas and the others. We wish to keep and observe it irrevocably together with the other articles, with deceit and fraud removed.

Diplomatic acts during the reign of Władysław Jagiełło, for the year 1413. (The Polish heading gives the same title and year.)
